title: Recovering from a pacemaker implantation | NHS inform
text:
Recovering from a pacemaker implantation
You’ll be able to feel a pacemaker, but you will soon get used to it. At first, it may seem heavy, and you may feel uncomfortable when you lie in certain positions.
You’ll usually have your pacemaker checked after 4 weeks at the hospital where it was put in. If this check is ok, you’ll have your pacemaker checked every 3 to 12 months.
If you’re not getting as much benefit as you imagined, your pacemaker may need some small adjustments. The specialist or cardiac technician can do this.
How will I be monitored?
You’ll be attached to a special monitor so the medical team can keep an eye on your heart rhythm. A chest
X-ray
will be done to check your lungs, as well as the position of the pacemaker and leads.
Will I be in pain after the procedure?
You may feel some pain or discomfort during the first 48 hours and will be given medication to ease this. There may also be some bruising where the pacemaker was inserted. This usually gets better within a few days. Tell the staff if your symptoms are persistent or severe.
Getting home from hospital
Most people can go home on the day they have a pacemaker fitted. You’ll need to arrange for someone to pick you up from the hospital and take you home.
Before you go home, you’ll be given a pacemaker registration card, which contains details of the make and model of your pacemaker. Always carry this with you in case of an emergency.
You may also wish to wear a MedicAlert bracelet or necklace engraved with important information. For example, the type of pacemaker you have, a personal identity number and a 24-hour emergency phone number.
How soon can I drive?
If you have an ordinary driving license and have had a pacemaker fitted, you can start driving again after one week, as long as you:
don’t have any symptoms, including dizziness or fainting, that can affect your driving
have regular check-ups in the pacemaker clinic
have not recently had a heart attack or heart surgery
Tell the
Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency
(DVLA) and your insurance company that you have a pacemaker.
If you drive a large or passenger-carrying vehicle, you’ll have to wait 6 weeks after your pacemaker is fitted before driving again. If you’ve had an ICD fitted you must be shock-free for 6 months.
How soon will I be back to normal?
You should be able to return to normal physical activities soon after surgery. It’s best to avoid reaching up on the side of your operation for 4 weeks. This means you should avoid hanging out washing or lifting anything from a high shelf.
It’s important to keep your arm mobile by gently moving it to avoid getting a frozen shoulder. A physiotherapist can show you how to do this.
You’ll usually be able to do all the things you want to do after around 4 weeks.
When can I exercise or play sports again?
You should avoid strenuous activities for 3 to 4 weeks after having a pacemaker fitted. After this, you should be able to do most activities and sports.
If you play contact sports, such as football or rugby, it’s important to avoid collisions. You may want to wear a protective pad. Check with your cardiologist before taking part in extremely energetic activities, such as squash.
How can I care for my wound?
Do not get your wound wet until your stitches have been taken out. After that, avoid wearing anything that rubs that area, such as braces. If you wear a bra, you may need a new one with wider straps.
Avoid exposing your wound to sunlight in the first year, as this can cause a darker scar.
Will I have to have my stitches removed?
Many doctors use soluble stitches that dissolve on their own. Before you go home, you’ll be told what type of stitches you have. If you need to have stitches removed, this will usually be after 10 days.
Will my pacemaker be affected by electrical equipment?
Most ordinary household electrical equipment is safe to use and will not interfere with your pacemaker. This includes microwaves, as long as they’re in good working order.
Specific advice is as follows:
mobile phones – it’s safe to use a mobile phone, but keep it away from your pacemaker
shop security systems – walking through these should not affect your pacemaker but don’t stand too close for long
airport security systems – don’t usually cause problems with pacemakers but tell staff that you have a pacemaker and carry your pacemaker identification card
MRI scan – these are not usually recommended for people with pacemakers due to their strong magnetic fields
Lithotripsy – this treatment for kidney stones must be avoided if you have a pacemaker
Speak to your healthcare team before returning to work if your job means you:
are in contact with strong electrical fields like arc welding or diathermy
work with high-power radio or TV transmitters
have direct contact with car ignition systems
